title: Part Two, Chapter 13: The Two Poor Dancers

verses.t: And on the fifth day they appeared again and were seen in the water by the people, where they looked like fish-men. And when they were seen by those of the underworld, they were searched for along the whole river. And on the next day two poor men appeared, poor in their faces and poor in all they had, their rags and clothes, and there was nothing of note in their faces. And then they were seen by those of the underworld; and what they did was little: only the dance of the pabay, of the weasel and of the armadillo, and of the Xtzul and the Chitic, were what they danced. And afterwards they did many wonders: they burned a house as if it were truly burning, and at once it was back as it had been; and many of those of the underworld watched in amazement. And then they cut each other to pieces; one of them would kill the other, and he lay as if dead, and then he would come back to life again; and all those of the underworld were amazed. And so they began to win over and defeat those of the underworld. And as soon as the news of their dancing reached the ears of the lords of the underworld, Hun-came and Vucub-came, they said when they heard it, "Who are these two poor men? Is it really so?" "Truly," said the one who brought the news to the lords, "their dancing and everything they do is a marvel." And hearing this with pleasure, they then sent their messengers to call them: "Let them come here and do it; they shall entertain us, and we shall admire and marvel at them. Tell them that the lords say so." This was said to the messengers, and they went to the dancers and gave them the message of the lords. "We do not want to," they said, "because we are afraid. Would they not insult us in the house of the lords, because our faces are ugly and we are poor? And is it not plain that we are only dancers? What shall we say to our poor companions who want our dancing and enjoy themselves with us? Are we to do it so for the lords? Well, and if we do not want to, messengers?" This is what Hun-ahpu and Xbalanque said. And their faces filled with bitterness and grief, and they went sorrowfully, because they did not want to go; and many times the messengers forced them, and gnashed their teeth in anger before those they had come for. And then they went before the lords. And they came before the lords, and went sadly, with bowed heads; and so they arrived and humbled themselves and bowed and prostrated themselves, all in rags, so that they truly looked like poor men. And then they were asked about their country and their people, and they were also asked about their fathers and mothers: "Where are you from? Where have you come from?" "We do not know, lord; we do not know the house of our fathers and mothers; we were very small when they died." This alone they said, and nothing else. "Very well. Come, make us enjoy ourselves. How much do you want for your work? We shall give it," it was said to the poor men. "We want nothing, for truly we are ashamed," they said to the lord. "Do not be afraid or ashamed. Dance, and first do that cutting of yourselves to pieces, and burn my house; do everything you know; we shall enjoy ourselves, for so our hearts desire. And you shall go, and we shall give you your price, for you are poor men," it was said to them. And then they began their song and their dance, and then all those of the underworld came to watch; they gathered to enjoy themselves. And they danced everything, the weasel, the pubay, the armadillo. And the lord said to them, "Come, cut this dog of mine to pieces, and bring it back to life," it was said to them. "Yes, lord," they said; and then they cut the dog to pieces and brought it back to life again, and the dog was very happy when they brought it back to life, and it wagged its tail. And the lord said to them, "Come, burn this house of mine!" And they burned the lord's house; and though all the lords were crowded together in the house, they were not burned; and then very quickly they brought the house back to what it was; not for an instant was the house of Hun-came lost. And all the lords marvelled, and they danced as well, and rejoiced greatly. And it was said to them by the lord, "Come, cut a man to pieces, and let him not die," it was said to them. "Very well," and taking a man, they cut him open and lifted up that man's heart on high and showed it before all the lords; and again Hun-came and Vucub-came marvelled. And in an instant they brought him back to life, and he was very glad when he was brought back to life; and the lords marvelled. "Come, now cut yourselves to pieces; we want to see this dance of yours," the lords said to them. "Very well," they said; and then they cut themselves to pieces. Hun-ahpu was cut up by Xbalanque, who divided him all into parts, his arms and legs; he cut off his head and threw it far away, and took out his heart, and it was thrown onto the grass; and all the lords of the underworld were drunk with watching it. And he alone was dancing, Xbalanque; and he said, "Come, get up!" and at once Hun-ahpu came back to life. Greatly the lords rejoiced, and kept on rejoicing; and they did this to delight Hun-came and Vucub-came, and they felt the joy as if they themselves were dancing.

And then a desire came upon the lords, their ruin, from this dance of Hun-ahpu and Xbalanque; and then the command came from Hun-came and Vucub-came: "Do this to us as well; cut us to pieces, cut us up one by one!" said Hun-came and Vucub-came to Hun-ahpu and Xbalanque. "Very well; rejoice. Did you not bring us here so that we might delight you, you who are lords over your vassals?" they said to the lords. And the first to be cut to pieces was the one who was head and lord of the underworld, called Hun-came; and when Hun-came was dead, Vucub-came was seized; and they did not bring them back to life. And then the others went running away when they saw the lords dead; they went running in great leaps, and both of them were opened up, and it was done only as a punishment. In an instant the lord died and did not come back to life. And a lord who had run away came before the dancers; they did not seize him; he begged for mercy when he was recognised. And all of them went off, all the vassals, to a great ravine, and all of them crowded into a great pit; and they were all crowded in there when countless ants came and went to sting them in the ravine, and so drove them out. And coming out, they all surrendered, since their lord of the underworld was already defeated. And only by wonder and miracle did the boys transform and change themselves when they did this. And then they told their names, and made themselves known before all those of the underworld.
